standard.title: Continuities and Changes in an Asian Society Around the Turn of the 20th Century
standard.description: continuities and changes and their effects on the ways of life and living conditions, political and legal institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century in an Asian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can apply the continuity-and-change framework (AC9HH9K05) and describe the effects of European contact (AC9HH9K20). They have not yet applied this framework systematically to their chosen Asian society across multiple domains simultaneously.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the position of the chosen Asian society in relation to other nations around 1900; describe how foreign influence and imperialism challenged and changed Asian societies; investigate what remained the same or changed as a result of contact with European powers; and compare relevant policy systems (e.g. Cultivation System and Ethical System in the Dutch East Indies).

nodes.label: The chosen society's position in the world around 1900
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the position of the chosen Asian society in relation to other nations around 1900 — including its relationship to European powers, its domestic political situation, and how ideas such as nationalism were influencing it.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the chosen society's relationship with European powers around 1900 and identify at least one way nationalism or reform ideas were shaping the society's development.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the chosen society's geopolitical position — China after the Boxer Rebellion and the unequal treaties; India under full British Raj administration with growing nationalist movement; Japan after the Meiji Restoration as an industrialising power; Indonesia under Dutch colonial administration; explain how ideas of nationalism and self-determination were beginning to influence political movements; describe what internal reform or resistance movements existed; explain how the chosen society's position compared to its position at the start of the period (from K19).
wider: Examine how the Russo-Japanese War (1905) — the first major victory of an Asian power over a European one — affected the political imagination of nationalist movements across Asia

Compare the position of two Asian societies around 1900 — examining what different trajectories (Japan's industrialisation vs China's partial reform vs India's nationalist emergence) reveal about what options were available to Asian societies facing European power
nodes.hinge_reason: Establishing the society's position around 1900 is the prerequisite for the continuity-change analysis. Students who do not understand where the society stood at this moment cannot systematically examine what changed and what persisted from the earlier period examined in K19 and K20.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly jump to describing changes without establishing the baseline position at the turn of the century. Explicitly situating the society in the world at this moment provides the reference point the continuity-change analysis requires.

success_criteria: Describes the chosen society's relationship with European powers around 1900
Identifies at least one way that ideas such as nationalism were shaping the society's development

nodes.label: Continuities and changes across multiple domains
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how foreign influence and imperialism changed the chosen Asian society — and what remained the same — across ways of life, political institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two changes and one continuity across different domains in the chosen society, applying the continuity-change framework.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply the continuity-change framework across all three domains named in the descriptor — ways of life and living conditions, political and legal institutions, cultural expression; describe changes from European influence — railways, telegraph, Western education, factory goods, administrative reforms; continuities — traditional family structures, religious practices, artistic traditions, language, local economies that persisted despite colonial disruption; examine specific policy systems as case studies (Cultivation System vs Ethical System in Dutch East Indies; Company rule vs Crown rule in India); explain how different social groups within the chosen society experienced change and continuity differently.
wider: Examine the Cultivation System and Ethical System in the Dutch East Indies as contrasting colonial policy approaches — evaluating what each prioritised and what effects each produced for Indonesian society

Investigate how the building of railways in India (or equivalent infrastructure in the chosen society) simultaneously produced economic integration, cultural displacement, and nationalist consciousness
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Dutch East Indies Cultivation vs Ethical System comparison, or the infrastructure-as-double-edged-sword analysis, provides genuine complexity that resists simple evaluation — the same colonial policy could be both materially constructive and culturally destructive simultaneously.

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to synthesise knowledge from K19, K20 and K21 into a systematic continuity-change analysis across multiple domains — coordinating content from multiple prior nodes.

success_criteria: Describes at least two changes and one continuity in the chosen society around the turn of the 20th century
Applies the continuity-change framework across at least two domains
